Thursday, 5 November, in the truck cab, on the road to Pitești. Mr Dan is studying for his second attempt at the C1. Costel has news.
Dan, I've made a decision. I've asked the company for international routes. To Spain.
To Spain? Have you thought it through? That's a lot of days away from home.
I know. I'm taking a risk. But I've been studying Spanish in this cab for two years. I want to use it for real.
I don't start until January. Before that I have to keep a promise: to take you to the exam on the 21st.
This time I'm not taking anything for granted. Last time I made the mistake of being overconfident.
This time you'll pay attention to every word. And if you lose the thread, think of Grandpa.
On purpose, from the start. I listened to him. To his lie.
Then I draw a conclusion: you'll pass this exam.
That conclusion doesn't have enough arguments. But I like it.

"correr un riesgo" = to take a risk
"cumplir una promesa" = to keep a promise

At the beginning of November, Mrs Ionescu finally made a decision. She called Ana over at the school gate and told her that she had thought about it, as she had promised Rosa Elena on the first day, and that the school management had agreed to launch a Spanish club on Friday afternoons, after lessons, from four to five. It would not be a subject, but an optional activity. The teacher would be herself, as she had studied a little Spanish at secondary school thirty years earlier. But there was a condition, she explained: she would need an assistant. Ana asked her who. Mrs Ionescu smiled and told her the assistant had already decided that on her own.

Six children signed up on the first Friday. Rosa Elena arrived with her camera, her "Real words and fake words" notebook and a toy lamp, which she placed on the teacher's desk without any explanation. She taught them to say "hola", "gracias" and "por fin". Then she explained to them, very seriously, that in Spanish there were words made from other words, the way houses are made from bricks. She gave them an example: "des" plus "lámpara" made "deslampar", which meant turning off a lamp knowing it will be lit again tomorrow. Mrs Ionescu, at the back of the class, didn't dare tell her that the word didn't exist. She made a note in her notebook.

Meanwhile, Costel had made another decision, the most important in years. One Monday morning he walked into the office of the head of the haulage company, with his provisional C1 certificate folded in his pocket, and asked for international routes. To Spain. The boss looked at him as if he had gone mad. He reminded him that he was nearly sixty, that for a long time he had only done short routes within Romania and that long routes were for young drivers. Costel answered that he knew, that he was taking a risk. But that he had been studying Spanish in the truck cab for two years, and now he wanted to use it for real, not just in exams.

The boss was silent for a while. Then he took a folder with the list of January routes out of the drawer. There was one nobody wanted: Bucharest–Valencia, every two weeks, with a load of furniture on the way out and oranges on the way back. Four days there, four back. The young drivers turned it down because they said it was too long and that in Spain they couldn't understand anyone. The boss asked him if he wanted it. Costel didn't hesitate for a second. Valencia was where his daughter and Álex lived. He said yes before the boss had finished the sentence. Then he went out to the car park, sat in the cab and stayed there for ten minutes without starting the engine.

Mr Dan was the first to find out, the following Thursday, in the cab, on the way to Pitești. He was silent for a moment. Then he asked him whether he had thought it through, because it was a lot of days away from home. Costel told him yes, that he had been thinking about it for two years, even if he hadn't known it. Mr Dan confessed that he would miss him on Thursdays. Costel replied that he didn't start until January, and that before that he had to keep a promise: to take him to the exam on the 21st. Mr Dan closed his exercise book, looked out of the window at the grey November fields and said that, in that case, he couldn't fail, because Costel would leave without seeing him pass.

That month, Mr Dan studied as he had never studied before, not even for his engineering degree. But this time he did it differently. He didn't make colour-coded tables. Ana had told him that at C1 level the problem wasn't grammar but naturalness: he spoke correct Spanish, but textbook Spanish. She suggested he pay attention to how native speakers combined words, not to the rules. So Mr Dan began writing down in a notebook the combinations he found in the newspapers: "tomar una decisión", "llevar a cabo", "hacer frente a", "sacar una conclusión". By the end of the month he had two hundred. He called them "the pairs".

His wife, the retired chemistry teacher, became his private examiner. Every evening after dinner she read him sentences from the newspapers aloud with a gap where the verb should be, and he had to guess what was missing. "The government has taken… a measure." "The police have carried… out an operation." "The team had to face… up to defeat." At first he got half of them wrong. After three weeks he hardly got any wrong. His wife told him it was very like chemistry: some elements combined and others didn't, and nobody really knew why, but if you mixed them wrongly, they exploded.

Ana explained to him one day, in her kitchen, that this was called collocations, and that it was the hardest thing in any language, because it had no logic. That in Romanian you "take" a decision and in Spanish you "tomas" it, and that no rule explained it. That in Romanian you "make" a mistake and in Spanish you "cometes" an error. That in Romanian you "pull" a conclusion and in Spanish you "sacas" it. Mr Dan said this was intolerable for an engineer. Ana answered that precisely for that reason they had to be learned by heart, in pairs, like ballroom dances. Mr Dan said that he did understand that, because he had danced the tango as a young man.

Ecaterina, who had come back from Triana on 22 October with the iron key hanging on a chain, received a letter from Inés that month. It was a proposal. Inés had made a decision and wanted Ecaterina to be the first to know: she wanted to launch a new book with her. It would be an anthology of the letters that had reached the newspaper after the article, the four hundred or so that were now in boxes at El Mostrador. They would only publish those whose writers gave permission. Ecaterina would choose the letters and write an introduction. Inés ended by saying she should not think she said this out of politeness: she believed nobody could carry it out better than her.

Ecaterina took a week to reply. Not because she doubted the book was worth it, but because she was afraid of not being worthy of those letters. They were letters from strangers who had kept something for years and had finally dared to send it. To her, publishing them felt like opening four hundred drawers belonging to other people. She said so to Ana one afternoon, on the balcony. Ana reminded her of what she herself had written in the article: that the letters we don't send are left waiting. And she suggested she think of those letters as if they were for others who hadn't dared yet. Ecaterina replied to Inés that same night. She said yes.

But she set a condition. She wrote to Inés that the book couldn't have her name on the cover, but the names of everyone who had written the letters, even if there were four hundred. And that the title had to be the article's, because it had been Marta's idea, and Marta deserved to appear somewhere. Inés replied the next day that four hundred names wouldn't fit on a cover, but they would fit on the endpapers, the first pages of the book, in small print. And that the title seemed perfect to her. Ecaterina asked when they would start. Inés told her they already had: on Monday Lola would send her the boxes in Bucharest by courier.

The boxes arrived on a rainy Thursday. There were seven of them, cardboard, tied with string, and the courier had to carry them up to the fourth floor two at a time, because the building's lift had been broken since September. Ecaterina put them in the living room, around the desk, and stood looking at them for a long time before opening the first. Inside, the letters were sorted by date, with a rubber band around every fifty, and on top of them all was a note from Lola: "I've read them all. I cried over a hundred and twelve. I counted. I'm leaving the lamp on for you, even if from afar." Ecaterina lit the little lamp in the living room, at seven, and opened the first letter.

In Madrid, Marta received Inés's reply about "La librera de Triana" on 12 November. It was long, with many corrections, but it began with a sentence that Marta read three times before going on: "We're publishing it in the spring." Inés wrote that the last chapter, the wedding, was the best thing she had ever written, precisely because it wasn't perfect: the priest arriving late, the shoes under the pew, the rings in the guitar case. She wrote that she had drawn a conclusion from her manuscript: that Marta wrote better when she stopped trying to write well. And she asked permission to use as the cover a photo by Andrei that she had seen in Begoña's office.

Marta called Andrei immediately. Andrei was at the agency, developing the photos for a feature on Madrid's markets. When Marta told him that Inés wanted the photo of Faustino's back for the cover, Andrei went so quiet that Marta thought the call had dropped. Then he asked her how the photo had got to Begoña's office. Marta didn't know. Andrei went to ask Begoña, who was at her desk with her glasses on the tip of her nose. Begoña didn't look up from the screen. She told him the photo was too good to stay in a drawer, and that she had no intention of apologising for sending it.

Andrei stood in front of her desk, not knowing what to say. Begoña reminded him that a year earlier, when he had arrived at the agency, she had told him that in this profession you had to take risks, and he had answered that he didn't like risks. "Well, there you go," she told him, "sometimes others take the risks for you." Then she patted him on the arm, the first time in fourteen months, and told him to go back to the darkroom, that the markets wouldn't develop themselves. Lucas, who had heard everything from the next desk, told Andrei afterwards that in Begoña's language that was a hug.

That evening Andrei called his father. It was Thursday, and Mr Dan had just come back from Costel's cab with his notebook of "pairs" under his arm. Andrei told him about the cover. His father was quiet for a moment, as he always was when something moved him and he didn't want it to show. Then he asked how many copies they would print and what size the photo would be, because he was an engineer and didn't know any other way of being happy. Andrei laughed. He told him he didn't know yet. His father then told him, in Spanish, slowly, that he was proud of him. Andrei replied that this was a perfect collocation.

In Triana, the newlyweds had found their routine in less than a month. Faustino got up at seven, went down to open the bookshop, arranged the books in the window and sat in the doorway in his red beret to chat with the neighbours passing by. Doña Remedios came down at nine, told him he had arranged the books badly, and rearranged them. Then they argued for an hour about Machado or Lorca, and at eleven they had coffee together under the orange tree. Curro wrote to Ecaterina that people in the neighbourhood said the bookshop now sold half as many books, but people stayed twice as long.

Faustino had also started a new custom. Every evening at seven, instead of lighting a lamp, he opened one of the bookshop's books at random and read aloud, in the doorway, the first sentence he came across. Sometimes two people stopped to listen; sometimes twenty. The neighbourhood children called him "the sentence man". Doña Remedios said it was Faustino's way of missing the Cuesta de Moyano without saying so. Faustino denied it. He said he didn't miss anything, that at his age you only missed what you hadn't lived yet, and that he was finally living it now.

On Saturday, 21 November, Mr Dan sat the C1 exam for the second time at the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest. Costel drove him there, as he had promised, and this time it was Costel who waited outside, in the café opposite, with a book he didn't read. Before going in, Mr Dan shook his hand, very formally, as if they were two engineers closing a contract. Costel told him to pay attention to every word and, if he lost the thread, to think of Grandpa. Mr Dan answered that there was no need, that he was going to think of Grandpa on purpose, from the start. He had listened to him. To his lie.

In the writing paper he got a topic that seemed made for him: an opinion article on whether older people should keep studying. Mr Dan smiled when he read it. He planned the text in five minutes, with the five boxes Costel had drawn for Ecaterina in August. He began with a clear thesis. He used three of his "pairs" in the first paragraph: "tomar una decisión", "correr un riesgo", "hacer frente a". As his main argument he gave the example of a ninety-seven-year-old man who had learned to read at thirty, in the army. He didn't give his name. But he wrote the whole text thinking of him, on the porch, under the walnut tree, with the lamp lit.

When he came out at six in the evening, after the oral exam, Costel was waiting for him at the door. He asked him how it had gone. Mr Dan said he didn't know, and that this time he wouldn't draw any conclusions until the results came out. But Costel had known him for two years, and he noticed something different in the way he walked. He asked him what he had got in the oral. Mr Dan told him the photo was of a truck on a snowy mountain road, and that he had had to imagine the driver's story. Costel burst out laughing. He asked him what story he had told. Mr Dan said: his, Costel's.

While he waited, Costel had spent six hours in the café opposite. He drank four coffees, ate two covrigi and called Ana three times to ask her whether a six-hour exam was normal. Ana reminded him that his own had lasted just as long. Costel said he didn't remember, that on that day he had been too nervous to look at the clock. In the middle of the afternoon, the waitress, a young woman who studied at the Instituto Cervantes, asked him whether he was waiting for someone sitting an exam. Costel told her yes, a friend, the best student he had ever known. The young woman asked him if he spoke Spanish too. Costel answered that he did, thanks to him.

He told the examiner the story of a Romanian trucker of nearly sixty who had learned Spanish in his cab, listening to audiobooks between Arad and Constanța, and who, when he finally spoke it well, had decided to ask for a route to Spain so he could see his grandson more often. The examiner asked whether the driver was afraid of the mountain road. Mr Dan told her no, that the driver was afraid of only one thing: not knowing what to say when he arrived. And that, in his experience, this happened to everyone who learned a language out of love, even if it was love for a grandson.

That night they didn't go straight back to Bucharest. Costel drove to Grandpa Gheorghe's village, because it had started snowing and Grandpa had asked them on the phone to tell him about the exam in person. They arrived at eight. The first snow of the year already covered the porch and the branches of the walnut tree, and the oil lamp was shining in the window. Grandpa was waiting for them by the stove, in his Sunday cap, although it was Saturday. He asked Mr Dan how it had gone. Mr Dan told him the truth: that he didn't know, but that he had heeded his lie. Grandpa laughed so hard he had to hold on to the table.

Then Grandpa asked Costel about the Valencia route. Costel explained that he started on 11 January, that it would be eight days every two weeks, and that in Valencia he would sleep at his daughter's, with Álex. Grandpa thought for a while. He asked whether there were walnut trees in Valencia. Costel told him he didn't know, that there were mostly orange trees there. Grandpa got up slowly, went to the pantry and came back with a bag of walnuts, like the one he had sent Faustino. He asked him to take it to Álex on his first trip. "So that he plants one," he said. "Orange trees bear fruit in three years. Walnut trees take ten. That's why you have to start early."

They stayed the night. Elena made up the room upstairs for them and gave them two down quilts, because the house was old and it was very cold at night. Mr Dan couldn't sleep. He went down to the kitchen at midnight and found Grandpa sitting in front of the window, watching the snow fall on the walnut tree, with the lamp lit. He sat down beside him without saying anything. They stayed like that for a long while. Then Grandpa told him, in Romanian, that he too had failed many things in life, though not reading. That he had failed as a father sometimes, and as a husband at other times. But that he had never stopped trying again the next day.

Mr Dan asked him what he did when he failed. Grandpa told him: the same thing he did every evening at seven: light the lamp and go on living. That he had learned that important things were not passed all at once, but little by little, the way walnut trees grow. And that, whatever happened with the exam, Mr Dan had already passed the hardest part, which was trying again without shame. Mr Dan didn't know what to answer. He stayed looking at the snow. Then he wrote Grandpa's sentence on the last page of his notebook of "pairs", under number two hundred: "light the lamp and go on living".

The next morning, when they came down to breakfast, the whole village was white. Costel went out onto the porch with a cup of coffee and came across Rosa Elena, who had arrived the evening before with her parents to see the snow and was taking photos of the walnut tree with her camera. He asked her what she was photographing. The girl explained that she was making a collection for the Friday Spanish club: photos of things that had no name in Romanian but did in Spanish, or the other way round. Costel asked her which one was for the snowy walnut tree. Rosa Elena thought for a moment and answered that she didn't know yet, but she would make one up.

Before going back to Bucharest, Mr Dan said goodbye to Grandpa on the porch. The snow had stopped and the morning sun made the branches of the walnut tree sparkle. Grandpa shook his hand and said a single word to him in Spanish, the last one he had learned, because Rosa Elena had taught it to him that very morning: "Ánimo." Mr Dan asked him where he had learned it. Grandpa pointed to the girl, who was photographing the snow from the barn door. Mr Dan wrote the word in his notebook, although he already knew it. Underneath he wrote: "two hundred and one". He said some words weren't anyone's pair, but they kept you company all the same.

That Sunday afternoon, back in Bucharest, Ecaterina opened letter number two hundred from the seven boxes. It had been written by a seventy-year-old woman from Valencia. She told how, for forty years, she hadn't dared tell her daughter she was proud of her, because in her family those things weren't said. That after reading the article she had written it to her in a letter, and that she hadn't posted it, but had slipped it into her daughter's handbag without her seeing. Her daughter had called her that very evening. Ecaterina read the letter twice. Then she put it on the pile of chosen ones and wrote in the margin: "the first".
"se había cortado la llamada" = the call had dropped

From all this we draw a conclusion.
A few lines from Mr Dan's notebook, with Ana's comments in the margin.
Number 1: tomar una decisión. Ana's note: in Romanian you "take" it, in Spanish you "tomas" it. Don't look for logic.
Number 47: hacer caso. Ana's note: it isn't "to make a case". It means listening to someone and doing what they say. Example: Mr Dan never listens to his wife.
